result:
Solution 3 is correct; Solutions 1 and 2 are not.

**Upper bound.** A set and its complement are disjoint, so P can hold at most one set from each of the 2^999 complementary pairs {A, S∖A}. If A is a transversal (one element from each pair {i, 1001−i}), then A′ = S∖A. Condition 3 would then force both A and S∖A into P, which violates condition 2. So neither set of such a complementary pair can be in P. There are 2^500 transversals, forming 2^499 such pairs. Hence |P| ≤ 2^999 − 2^499.

**Construction.** Take all sets of size at least 501. Any two of these intersect, and reflection preserves size. Among the 500-element sets, exclude the transversals. From each remaining complementary pair, pick one set, choosing consistently so that A′ is picked whenever A is. This is possible because, for a non-transversal A, the set A′ is not the complement of A. Two 500-element sets are disjoint only if they are complementary, and the selection avoids that. A 500-element set always meets a set of size at least 501, since 500 + 501 > 1000. The family therefore has exactly 2^999 − 2^499 members, so the bound is attained.

**Checking each solution.**
- Solution 1 gives a smaller family, because it takes only the 500-sets containing one fixed pair. Its answer is not the maximum.
- Solution 2 claims 2^999, which exceeds the proven upper bound, so it is wrong.
- Solution 3 gives 2^999 − 2^499, which matches the bound and the construction.

VERDICT 1: REJECT
VERDICT 2: REJECT
VERDICT 3: ACCEPT
